title: First argument: worship without God's word is will-worship
source_text: LVII. Porro Beatos Spiritus sive hominum, sive Angelorum, non esse colendos eo cultu qui ipsis in Ecclesia Romana exhibetur, dum scilicet, aedes sacrae & altaria in eorum honorem construuntur atque dedicantur, cerei illis accenduntur, incensum adoletur, & coram ipsis tanquam intuentibus genua flectuntur: dum vota eis nuncupantur, & variae fiunt illis oblationes, ac juramenta per eorum nomen concipiuntur: dum denique precibus solennibus ad eorum auxilium & opem confugitur, & hymni illis publice canuntur in gratiarum actionem pro beneficiis a Deo acceptis, & si qua sunt hujusmodi: nec Angelos, inquam, beatos, nec Sanctos in Christo defunctos eo modo colendos esse, inde probant primum Protestantes, quod talis cultus non debuit ab hominibus sine Dei verbo excogitari. Alioqui sine fide exhibebitur: cum absque Dei verbo nemo certus esse possit illum Deo gratum & acceptum esse. Adeoque si constet ejusmodi cultum nullo Dei praecepto & revelatione niti, inter ἐθελοθρησκείας ab Apostolo damnatas merito rejici potest. Jam vero totum illum cultum in Dei verbo nullum fundamentum habere, ex eo patet, quod in universa Scriptura seu Veteris, seu Novi Testamenti, nullum ejus extat praeceptum, aut exemplum.
pass_a_gloss: Further, that the Blessed Spirits, whether of men or of Angels, are not to be worshipped with that worship which is shown to them in the Roman Church, while namely sacred buildings and altars are constructed and dedicated in their honor, candles are lit to them, incense is burned, and before them as if looking on the knees are bent: while vows are pronounced to them, and various offerings are made to them, and oaths are conceived by their name: while finally with solemn prayers one flees to their aid and help, and hymns are publicly sung to them in thanksgiving for benefits received from God, and whatever things are of this kind: that neither the blessed Angels, I say, nor the Saints who died in Christ are to be worshipped in that way, the Protestants prove first from this, that such worship ought not to have been devised by men without the word of God. Otherwise it will be shown without faith: since without the word of God no one can be certain that it is pleasing and acceptable to God. And so if it is established that worship of this kind rests on no precept and revelation of God, it can deservedly be rejected among the will-worships condemned by the Apostle. But now that that whole worship has no foundation in the word of God is evident from this, that in the whole Scripture whether of the Old or of the New Testament, no precept of it exists, nor example.
pass_b_english: The Protestants hold that the blessed spirits, whether of men or of angels, are not to be honored with the worship the Roman Church gives them: churches and altars built and dedicated in their honor, candles lit to them, incense burned, knees bent before them as though they were watching; vows made to them, offerings of every kind presented, oaths sworn by their name; and, finally, solemn prayers by which people run to them for help, and hymns sung to them publicly in thanksgiving for benefits received from God, and anything else of the kind.

Neither the blessed angels, I say, nor the saints who have died in Christ are to be worshiped in this way. The Protestants prove it first from the fact that such worship ought not to have been devised by human beings apart from God's word. Otherwise it will be offered without faith, since without God's word no one can be sure that it pleases God and is accepted by him.

So if it is clear that worship of this kind rests on no command or revelation of God, it may rightly be rejected as one of the forms of self-made worship that the Apostle condemns. And it is plain that this whole worship has no foundation in God's word, since in all of Scripture, Old Testament or New, there is no command for it and no example of it.

lemmas.gloss: it will be shown (offered) without faith

choices.why: Colossians 2:23; 'self-made worship' renders the Greek compound in plain English.
